notes.meaning: News traveled fast. Believers all over Judea heard that Gentiles (people who were not Jewish) had welcomed God's word, the good news about Jesus. This was a big surprise. Many Jewish believers had assumed Gentiles would not be open to the gospel.

When Peter got back to Jerusalem, some Jewish believers who held tightly to circumcision and the Jewish law challenged him. They were upset that he went into a Gentile's home and ate with Gentiles. Jewish custom saw that as making a person unclean. Several commentators point out that the church felt free to question Peter. So they did not see him as a ruler who was above correction.
Peter did not get angry or pull rank. He simply told them what had happened, step by step. Telling the plain facts calmly is often the best way to clear up a misunderstanding.

Peter retells the vision he had while praying in Joppa. He adds that the sheet came "right down to me" and that he studied it closely. This shows the vision was meant for him in particular. Peter later understood that it was really about people, not only about food.
A voice told Peter to kill and eat. Peter refused, because he had never eaten food the Law of Moses called unclean. By telling this, Peter shows his critics that he had felt exactly as they did.

God said not to call anything impure that He had made clean. God had changed the situation, so Peter could not be blamed for changing his mind. The vision came three times and then went back up into heaven. Both details showed it truly came from God.

At that very moment, men sent by Cornelius arrived. The Spirit told Peter to go with them without holding back. Some Bible copies read "making no distinction" between Jew and Gentile. Peter took six Jewish brothers along as witnesses, and they were standing there to back up his story.

Cornelius had seen an angel who told him to send for Peter. Peter would bring a message by which Cornelius and his whole household would be saved. So even a man who worshiped God still needed to hear about Jesus. The gospel is the means God uses to bring people to salvation.

While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came on the Gentiles, just as He had come on the first believers at Pentecost. This settled the question. Peter rested his case on what God did, not on what he himself said. It was God's stamp of approval.

Peter remembered Jesus' promise: John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is Christ's own gift. A minister can give the outward sign of water, but only Christ gives the inner work of the Spirit. Peter now saw that this promise was for all who believe, both Jews and Gentiles.

God gave the Gentiles the same gift He gave the Jewish believers. He gave it because they believed, not because they were circumcised. So how could Peter refuse to baptize people God had already filled with His Spirit? Getting in the way of that would mean standing against God himself.

The critics went quiet and began praising God. They saw that God had given Gentiles "repentance unto life." Repentance means turning from sin to God, and it leads to new and eternal life. Repentance is God's gift: He changes a hard heart into a soft one.

The story goes back to the believers who fled Jerusalem after Stephen was killed. They took the gospel to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch. God used persecution meant to hurt the church to spread the good news. At first they spoke only to Jews, because they did not yet understand that Gentiles were included.

Some believers from Cyprus and Cyrene began telling Greeks, meaning non-Jews, about the Lord Jesus. This was something new and bold. Ordinary believers, not apostles, were the ones who took this step. Jesus himself was the center of their message.

"The hand of the Lord" means God's power working through them and opening people's hearts. Many believed and turned to the Lord. Real faith changes how a person lives, and that change comes from God, not from the preacher's skill.

The church in Jerusalem heard the news and sent Barnabas to Antioch. He came from Cyprus himself and was known as a "son of encouragement," so he was a wise choice. He went to look into the new work and to help it grow.

Barnabas saw clear signs of God's grace (His free, undeserved kindness) in the new believers, and he was glad. He did not stir up arguments about circumcision. Instead he urged them all to stay close to the Lord with a firm, settled heart. New faith needs steady encouragement to last.

differ.view: God gives the grace, but believers must use it and keep holding on. Someone who stops clinging to the Lord can fall from grace and lose salvation.

notes.meaning: Luke explains why Barnabas acted this way. He was a good, kind and big-hearted man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. He rose above narrow prejudice, and many more people came to the Lord.

Barnabas went to Tarsus and searched for Saul. He brought him to Antioch, even though Saul might outshine him. For a whole year they taught the church and many others. In Antioch the believers were first called "Christians," meaning followers of Christ, the Anointed One. Who first used the name is not certain, but believers came to wear it with honor.

Prophets came from Jerusalem. These were people the Spirit inspired to teach and sometimes to tell what would happen. One of them, Agabus, said by the Spirit that a great famine would hit "the whole world," meaning the Roman Empire. This was not a guess but a message from God. It came true under Emperor Claudius, and historians of the time record it.

The believers in Antioch decided that each would give what they could to help the believers in Judea. They gave freely, out of love and thankfulness to the people who had brought them the gospel. They did what they planned. They sent the gift to the church elders (leaders) through Barnabas and Saul.
